title: The Wrong Side and the Right Side: from Belcourt to Le Grand Fossard
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Belcourt: the Poverty and the Sun

stops.name: Dréan, the birth at Mondovi
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is firm, the pin is town-level. Dréan, ex-Mondovi, is at 36.6833 / 7.7500 per en.wikipedia; the exact house is not identified in any source reached, and an earlier working coordinate of 36.7333 / 7.7667 was 5.5 km off.
stops.campa: In a farm settlement on the Bône plain, twenty-five kilometers south of Annaba, a second son is born to Lucien Auguste Camus, a cellarman for a wine shipper, and Catherine Hélène Sintès, who is deaf and cannot read. The village is called Mondovi; independent Algeria will rename it Dréan. They are poor settlers, French by law and Spanish through the mother, with no property, no books, and no expectation that a child born among these vineyards will leave them. He is registered on the seventh of November 1913.
suggested_refs: The commune of Dréan, ex-Mondovi, El Taref province, Algeria

stops.name: Saint-Brieuc, the father dies in the auxiliary hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrects the common English formula that Lucien Camus died at the Marne: fr.wikipedia gives the wounding at the Marne in September and the death on 11 October 1914 in the auxiliary hospital of the rue Saint-Benoît at Saint-Brieuc, where he is buried.
stops.campa: Lucien Camus, mobilized into a Zouave regiment at the outbreak of the war, takes a shell splinter in the head at the First Battle of the Marne in September and is evacuated across France to Brittany. He dies on the eleventh of October in the auxiliary military hospital on the rue Saint-Benoît at Saint-Brieuc and is buried in the town. What his son will ever have of him is a photograph and a regimental record, and a name he has to take on trust. The son is eleven months old on the day of the death.
suggested_refs: The military plot at Saint-Brieuc holding the grave of Lucien Auguste Camus, visited in the opening chapters of Le Premier Homme

stops.name: Algiers, the rooms on the rue de Lyon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move and the quarter; the pin is the modern rue Mohamed Belouizdad, ex-rue de Lyon, geocoded by Nominatim. The exact building is unverified, and the family's 1921 move within the same street to number 93 is folded into this stop rather than pinned separately four metres away.
stops.campa: The widow takes her two boys to Algiers, to the working quarter of Belcourt, into an apartment on the rue de Lyon shared with her mother and her brother. Catherine Camus cleans houses and speaks little; the grandmother rules the rooms and beats the children; there is no running water, no lamp of one's own, and not one book. What the boy has instead of a library is the quarter: the sea at the end of the street, the heat coming off the pavement, football on packed earth. In 1921 the family moves again, within the same street, to number 93.
suggested_refs: Rue Mohamed Belouizdad, ex-rue de Lyon, in the Belouizdad district of Algiers, ex-Belcourt

stops.name: Belcourt, the schoolmaster who would not let it go
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, approximate as a place and a date. Britannica and the IEP both carry Germain and the scholarship; the exact site of the école communale of the rue Aumerat was not verified, and this pin is a district-level approximation on that street's line.
stops.campa: In the primary school on the rue Aumerat a teacher named Louis Germain notices that the boy from the rue de Lyon works faster than the rest, and keeps him after hours without charge to prepare the scholarship examination. The grandmother wants him out of school at fourteen and earning. Germain walks to the apartment and argues her down in her own kitchen. Thirty-four years later, in the week the Nobel Prize is announced, the first letter Camus writes is to Germain.
suggested_refs: Camus's 1957 letter to Louis Germain, printed as an appendix to the Gallimard edition of Le Premier Homme

stops.name: Bab El Oued, the scholarship boy in goal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school and the football; the pin corrects a working coordinate that had duplicated the University of Algiers. The Grand Lycée, ex-lycée Bugeaud, today lycée Émir-Abdelkader, is at 36.7887 / 3.0605 per Nominatim.
stops.campa: He enters the Grand Lycée at Bab El Oued on a scholarship, a charity boy among the sons of colonial functionaries, and learns to carry two tongues: the school's French and the flat quick speech of Belcourt, which he does not use in class. He keeps goal for the junior side of the Racing Universitaire d'Alger and is good enough that for some years football, not literature, is what he expects of himself. He takes his baccalauréat in June 1932, by then already placing pieces in the small Algiers review Sud.
suggested_refs: Lycée Émir-Abdelkader, ex-lycée Bugeaud, Boulevard Ouanouri Mohamed, Bab El Oued, Algiers

stops.name: Algiers, the blood at the Hôpital Mustapha
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia dates the first attack to December 1930. Coordinates corrected to the Hôpital Mustapha Pacha per Nominatim; a working coordinate of 36.7539 / 3.0674 was 1.5 km off.
stops.campa: In December, at seventeen, he coughs blood and is taken to the Hôpital Mustapha, where the diagnosis is tuberculosis of the right lung. In 1930 there is no cure for it. The treatment is rest, altitude, and air pumped into the pleural cavity, repeated for years. Football ends that winter, and he is told to arrange his life around a lung. The disease comes back in 1936, in 1942 and in 1949, and each return moves him to a different climate and a different house.
suggested_refs: Hôpital Mustapha Pacha, rue Aouchi Salah, Sidi M'Hamed, Algiers

stops.name: Algiers, the butcher's library on the rue du Languedoc
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia for the move and for Acault's role; the month is an ordering convention, and the street address is as given in the sources without an independent geocode.
stops.campa: Because the Belcourt apartment is crowded and damp and the doctors want him out of it, he moves in with his mother's brother, Gustave Acault, a butcher, a freethinker, and a reader. The shop pays for the house and the house holds a library: Gide on the shelves, Nietzsche, the Greeks, and an uncle who argues Voltaire across the table between deliveries. Camus arrives from rooms without a single book. He will spend his working life on questions Nietzsche asked first, and will answer most of them differently.
suggested_refs: The household of Gustave Acault, butcher, rue du Languedoc, Algiers

segments.name: The University, the Party, and the Théâtre du Travail

stops.name: Algiers, Plotinus and Saint Augustine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the studies and the 1936 diplôme; the 1933 date orders the segment. Coordinates are campus-level for the University of Algiers, per en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: He registers at the Faculté des Lettres to read philosophy and works his way through the degree in bad health, taking it in the intervals the lung allows. The diplôme he submits in 1936 is a study of Plotinus and Saint Augustine, Neoplatonism and Christian metaphysics: two Africans of the Roman province who wrote about a world beyond this one. Camus does not believe in that world. He spends a year of his twenties reading, closely and without hostility, the men from his own coast who did.
suggested_refs: Camus's 1936 diplôme d'études supérieures, 'Métaphysique chrétienne et néoplatonisme'

stops.name: Algiers, the marriage to Simone Hié
stops.date_confidence: contested and left contested. fr.wikipedia gives the marriage as June 1934 and the divorce as 1940; other summaries say 1935 and that the marriage was dissolved within a year. The separation of 1936 is common to both accounts. City-centre pin; the ceremony site is not named in the sources reached.
stops.campa: He marries Simone Hié in June 1934. She is beautiful, she is young, and she is addicted to morphine, first prescribed for menstrual pain and afterwards obtained however it can be obtained. Camus tries to get her off it and fails. He learns that she has been sleeping with the doctor who writes her prescriptions. They separate in 1936; the divorce is not pronounced until 1940. He is twenty and then twenty-one through all of it. For the rest of his life he says almost nothing about her in print, and the notebooks he keeps in these years mention her hardly at all.
suggested_refs: The Camus-Hié marriage of 1934, separation 1936, divorce 1940

stops.name: Algiers, the party card and the expulsion
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fact, contested for the dates. fr.wikipedia gives joining in 1935 and expulsion in 1937; Britannica says early 1935; en.wikipedia says he left a year after joining. The month here is an ordering convention.
stops.campa: He joins the Algerian section of the French Communist Party in 1935 and is sent to organize among Muslim Algerians in the quarters next to his own. The work suits him. The discipline does not. When the line shifts and the party drops its support for Algerian nationalist demands in the interest of a French popular front, he refuses to follow and keeps saying so in public, at meetings and in print. The expulsion is pronounced in 1937. He is twenty-three years old and has held a party card for two years.
suggested_refs: The Algerian section of the PCF and its 1936-1937 reversal on nationalist demands

stops.name: Algiers, the play the mayor would not allow
stops.date_confidence: attested. Corrects the widespread claim that Révolte dans les Asturies was staged and was his first produced work: fr.wikipedia records that it was censored by the mayor of Algiers and 'n'est pas représentée', printed by Charlot in May 1936 without author names, and first performed only in 2011-2012.
stops.campa: With a group of young leftists he founds the Théâtre du Travail, a workers' company that puts Malraux and Aeschylus in front of audiences who have never been inside a theatre. Their first piece is written by four hands, his among them: Révolte dans les Asturies, on the rising of the Spanish miners. The mayor of Algiers bans it before it can be played. Edmond Charlot prints it in May 1936 with no author's name on the title page, and it waits seventy-five years for a stage.
suggested_refs: Révolte dans les Asturies, Éditions Charlot, Algiers, May 1936, published anonymously

stops.name: Tipasa, the columns in the wormwood
stops.date_confidence: attested for the repeated visits through the later 1930s; the single date orders the segment. Noces was published by Charlot in 1939, not 1938 as some summaries have it.
stops.campa: Sixty kilometers west of Algiers the Roman town of Tipasa lies open to the sea, columns in the wormwood, mosaic floors under grass, the water showing through the gaps in the walls. Camus comes here through his twenties, alone and with friends, to swim and to lie in the sun among stones two thousand years abandoned. Out of it comes Noces, printed by Charlot in 1939: four essays arguing, against every metaphysics he has just spent a year studying, that this world is the only one and that it is enough.
stops.quote: Je comprends ici ce qu'on appelle gloire : le droit d'aimer sans mesure.
stops.quote_source: Albert Camus, 'Noces à Tipasa', in Noces (Charlot, Algiers, 1939), as quoted on en.wikipedia, 'Tipasa'
suggested_refs: The Roman ruins of Tipasa on the Algerian coast, a UNESCO World Heritage site

stops.name: Algiers, the first book
stops.date_confidence: attested; Britannica gives May 1937 for L'Envers et l'Endroit, published by Edmond Charlot in Algiers. City-centre pin for Charlot's press.
stops.campa: Edmond Charlot, who runs a bookshop and a small press in Algiers, brings out Camus's first book in May 1937: five essays on the death of his grandmother, on old people put aside by their families, on a hotel room in Prague, on the light over Algiers. The title means the wrong side and the right side, and the book insists on holding the two together, poverty and sunlight in one hand. He is twenty-three, and he will keep the thing out of print for the next twenty years.
suggested_refs: L'Envers et l'Endroit, Éditions Charlot, Algiers, May 1937

segments.name: Alger républicain: the Trade of Reporting

stops.name: Algiers, the courtroom benches
stops.date_confidence: attested for the appointment in October 1938 under Pascal Pia; the office pin is approximate for central Algiers and was not verified against an address.
stops.campa: Pascal Pia hires him onto a new left-wing daily and Camus learns the trade quickly: literary reviews first, then the courts. The lyricism of Noces falls away in these columns. What replaces it is a flat declarative sentence, stated once and not decorated, the sentence L'Étranger will be built out of four years later. He sits through the trials of Algerians prosecuted under colonial law and writes them up so plainly that the administration begins complaining about him by name.
suggested_refs: The court reporting of Alger républicain, 1938-1939, collected in Camus a Combat and in the Pléiade Oeuvres complètes

stops.name: Tizi Ouzou, the misery of the Kabylie
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia dates the series 5-15 June 1939. The pin is Tizi Ouzou, standing for an itinerary through Grande Kabylie; a working coordinate of 36.4667 / 4.9000 fell near Bouira, outside the region reported.
stops.campa: In June he travels the mountains of Grande Kabylie, through Tizi-Ouzou and Fort-National and Michelet, and files a series under the title Misère de la Kabylie. He reports the wage a Kabyle laborer is paid, the price of grain against it, children eating roots, schools that were voted and never built, relief that was announced and never delivered. He names the colonial administration as the cause, in a French newspaper, in French Algeria. The series runs from the fifth to the fifteenth of June 1939.
suggested_refs: Misère de la Kabylie, Alger républicain, 5-15 June 1939, later collected in Chroniques algériennes

stops.name: Algiers, the second paper banned
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sequence, approximate for the day. fr.wikipedia records Alger républicain suppressed in October 1939, Le Soir républicain founded in September 1939 and banned in January 1940. The day is an ordering convention.
stops.campa: War censorship closes Alger républicain in October 1939. Camus and Pia at once bring out an evening successor, Le Soir républicain, and run it with almost no staff and a censor reading every column before it goes to the stone. In January 1940 that paper is banned too, and the Government General makes it understood that he is not to be hired. Camus is twenty-six years old, the best-known young journalist in the country, and unemployable in it. Pia, who has gone ahead to Paris, writes on his behalf to a newspaper there.
suggested_refs: Le Soir républicain, Algiers, September 1939 to January 1940, edited by Camus and Pascal Pia

segments.name: The Exodus, the Absurd, and the Plateau

stops.name: Paris, the night desk at Paris-Soir
stops.date_confidence: attested for the March 1940 arrival and the post; the pin is approximate for the Paris newspaper district. The claim that he was carrying three books in draft, novel, essay and play, is standard in the biographies and not independently confirmed here.
stops.campa: In March he crosses the Mediterranean for the first time and takes a job as a layout secretary at Paris-Soir, a mass-circulation daily whose politics he despises and whose pages he assembles at night. In his luggage are three unfinished books: a novel, an essay, and a play. He mentions them to nobody at the paper. He lodges alone in a hotel, cold and homesick, and lists in his notebooks what is missing: the light, the sea, the heat coming off stone.
suggested_refs: Paris-Soir, the largest-circulation French daily of the late 1930s, where Camus worked as secrétaire de rédaction

stops.name: Lyon, the marriage in the middle of the flight
stops.date_confidence: attested; Britannica gives 3 December 1940 at Lyon. Corrects a working entry that placed the wedding at Oran, which is where Francine Faure was from, not where they married. The Clermont-Ferrand leg of the flight, summer 1940, is stated in the campa rather than pinned.
stops.campa: When the German army reaches Paris in June the paper folds its staff into cars and runs south, to Clermont-Ferrand first, where they spend the summer, and then to Lyon in the autumn: one household inside the largest civilian flight in French history. In Lyon, on the third of December 1940, Camus marries Francine Faure, a mathematician and pianist from Oran. He has told her plainly, before and after, that he does not believe in marriage and is not built for fidelity. She marries him anyway.
suggested_refs: The June 1940 exodus and the removal of the Paris press to Clermont-Ferrand and Lyon

stops.name: Oran, the city he could not like
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia dates the dismissal from Paris-Soir to January 1941 and the Oran teaching to 1941 through August 1942. Earlier summaries dating the return to 1940 are wrong.
stops.campa: Paris-Soir lets him go in January in a round of economies, and the couple return to Algeria, to Francine's family in Oran. He teaches in private schools; her family feeds them. He detests the town, which trades with its back to the sea and shows a traveler nothing but dust and commerce and closed shutters. He walks it anyway, street by street, and fills notebooks with the geometry of it. Six years later he will shut its gates in a novel and fill it with plague.
suggested_refs: Oran, the setting Camus mapped in 1941 and used for La Peste

stops.name: Paris, Gallimard prints the Absurd
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the publisher; the month orders the pair. The frequently repeated claim that the chapter on Kafka was cut from Le Mythe de Sisyphe to satisfy the German censor is standard in the literature and was not confirmed against a fetched source.
stops.campa: In occupied Paris, with a German censor's approval on the file, Gallimard publishes L'Étranger and then Le Mythe de Sisyphe in the same year. A novel about a man who shoots an Arab on a beach and is condemned for not weeping at his mother's funeral, and an essay that opens by asking whether life is worth living, reach the bookshops within months of each other. In February 1943 Jean-Paul Sartre reviews the novel in Cahiers du Sud, at length and in its favour.
stops.quote: There is but one truly serious philosophical problem and that is suicide.
stops.quote_source: Le Mythe de Sisyphe (1942), opening line, Justin O'Brien translation (1955), as quoted on en.wikiquote
suggested_refs: Gallimard's 1942 editions of L'Étranger and Le Mythe de Sisyphe
Kamel Daoud, Meursault, contre-enquête (2013), which retells L'Étranger from the side of the murdered man
Matthew Ward's 1988 translation, closer to the French than Stuart Gilbert's 1946 version

stops.name: Le Panelier, the plateau that hid people
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay; fr.wikipedia confirms only that Camus came to Le Chambon in 1942-1943 for his tuberculosis. The pin is the hamlet of Le Panelier north-east of the village; a working coordinate of 44.9569 / 4.2481 fell 12 km south.
stops.campa: Sent to the Massif Central in August for a relapse of the lung, he takes a room at a farm called Le Panelier above Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, on a Protestant plateau whose pastors and farmers are at that moment hiding Jewish refugees in their barns and attics. He stays two winters at the farm and writes most of the book about a quarantined town. In November the Allies land in North Africa, the Germans occupy the southern zone, and the sea between him and Algiers closes. His wife and his mother are on the far side of it.
suggested_refs: The hamlet of Le Panelier and the rescue network of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon, 1942-1943

segments.name: Combat: the Clandestine Years and the Liberation

stops.name: Paris, the paper printed at night
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month orders the segment. The pseudonym Beauchard is standard in the biographies and not confirmed against a fetched source. The pin is approximate for the newspaper district.
stops.campa: He comes down to Paris and into the Resistance network Combat, editing and writing for a sheet printed clandestinely and passed from hand to hand under a name that is not his. Nothing he writes underground carries his signature, and the name that comes down in the biographies, Beauchard, rests on no document. He meets Sartre and Beauvoir in this circle and is absorbed into it. The same year Gallimard takes him on as a reader, an office he keeps until he dies.
suggested_refs: Combat, clandestine edition, 1943-1944

stops.name: Paris, Le Malentendu at the Mathurins
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia gives the premiere as 24 June 1944 at the Théâtre des Mathurins, directed by Marcel Herrand, with María Casarès as Martha. That her father had been prime minister of the Spanish Republic is well established but outside the verified pool used here.
stops.campa: Le Malentendu opens on the twenty-fourth of June at the Théâtre des Mathurins: a mother and daughter who keep an inn murder their guests for money, and kill, without recognizing him, the son who has come home rich and would not say his own name. Occupied Paris does not care for it. Martha is played by María Casarès, twenty-one years old, a Spanish republican exile. That month she and Camus begin an affair which breaks off, resumes, and runs to the last week of his life.
suggested_refs: Le Malentendu, Théâtre des Mathurins, June 1944
Correspondance inédite 1944-1959, the Camus-Casarès letters, published 2017

stops.name: Paris, the editorials of the Liberation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the August 1944 emergence of Combat into the former offices of L'Intransigeant and for Camus's editorship. Circulation figures are widely quoted but were not verified here, hence the vague formulation in the campa.
stops.campa: Combat comes above ground during the insurrection of August and takes the presses and offices of a collaborationist evening paper. Camus writes the leaders, signed now, while the shooting is still going on in the streets: on what the purge of collaborators may and may not do, on justice as against vengeance, on the fact that a country an hour out of occupation is capable of anything. In the days after Hiroshima, the following August, he writes on the atomic bomb. He is thirty years old. Circulation runs into six figures.
suggested_refs: Combat, Paris, August 1944 onward, in the former offices of L'Intransigeant

stops.name: Algiers, the crisis he reported and the massacre he missed
stops.date_confidence: attested and deliberately re-pinned. The trip ran through April 1945 and the Combat series 'Crise en Algérie' ran 13-23 May 1945; fr.wikipedia's article on the Sétif massacres confirms both. Camus was not an eyewitness at Sétif, so no Sétif pin is used and the stop stays at Algiers.
stops.campa: He goes back to Algeria in April and travels the country to report what the war has done to it: famine in the countryside, wheat rationed away from Muslim Algerians, a political settlement promised in Paris and not delivered anywhere. Between his return and his first article, the army and the police kill thousands at Sétif and Guelma after a demonstration turns violent. He is not there and does not see it. The series runs in Combat from the thirteenth to the twenty-third of May, and he is read as a moderate.
suggested_refs: Crise en Algérie, Combat, 13-23 May 1945
The Sétif, Guelma and Kherrata massacres of May 1945
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Massacres de Sétif, Guelma et Kherrata'

stops.name: Paris, Caligula at the Hébertot
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia gives the Paris premiere as 26 September 1945 at the Théâtre Hébertot with Gérard Philipe, after a first performance at the Comédie de Genève in June 1945. The twins' birth in September 1945 is attested by Britannica and is stated here rather than given a pin of its own.
stops.campa: Caligula, written in 1938 and left in a drawer through the war, opens in Paris on the twenty-sixth of September at the Théâtre Hébertot with Gérard Philipe, twenty-two years old, as the emperor who reasons that since men die and are not happy he will have the moon brought to him. Earlier the same month Francine has given birth to twins, Catherine and Jean. Their father spends that autumn between the rehearsal room, the paper and Casarès. The notices make Philipe a star overnight.
suggested_refs: Caligula, Théâtre Hébertot, Paris, 26 September 1945, dir. Paul Oettly, with Gérard Philipe

segments.name: The Crossing: America and the Río de la Plata

stops.name: New York, the crisis of man at Columbia
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the venue per en.wikipedia; the verifying pass could not independently confirm the wider itinerary of the American tour, which is therefore left unpinned.
stops.campa: He crosses to New York in March on a French cultural mission and speaks at Columbia University on the crisis of man, to a hall of students whose country has just won a war. What he tells them is that the century has produced a new kind of person: one who can order a killing by telephone and never see the body, and who is not a monster but a functionary. The hall is full. He is thirty-two years old and has never before been out of Europe or Africa.
suggested_refs: 'The Crisis of Man', lecture at Columbia University, 28 March 1946

stops.name: New York, meeting Victoria Ocampo
stops.date_confidence: attested in victoria_ocampo.journey.json, from which this pin and date are inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo, who has already put Caligula into Spanish for the review Sur in Buenos Aires, is in New York, and the two meet for the first time in the flesh. What begins is fourteen years of friendship and correspondence between an Argentine publisher of independent means and an Algerian orphan who edits a Resistance paper, held together by a common refusal of every totalitarianism the century has on offer, of the right and of the left. She keeps his letters, all of them, from the first year to the last.
stops.quote: Su teléfono es tan sordo como Dios Padre. (Your telephone is as deaf as God the Father.)
stops.quote_source: Camus to Victoria Ocampo, in their correspondence, as carried in victoria_ocampo.journey.json
suggested_refs: The Camus-Ocampo correspondence, 1946-1960
Sur, Buenos Aires, which published Ocampo's Spanish Caligula

stops.name: Paris, the plague in Oran
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month orders the segment. Sales figures for the first printing are widely quoted and were not verified here.
stops.campa: Gallimard publishes La Peste in 1947: a chronicle of a plague year in Oran told by a doctor who refuses both despair and consolation and simply goes on working his rounds. He began it on the plateau at Le Panelier in the winter of the closed frontier and finishes it five years later. Everyone reads the occupation into it, which is right and not sufficient. The book is also about Oran, where he taught school and was miserable, and about a disease that came for his own lungs at seventeen and has never gone away. He is thirty-three the year it appears.
stops.quote: The evil that is in the world always comes of ignorance, and good intentions may do as much harm as malevolence, if they lack understanding.
stops.quote_source: La Peste (1947), as quoted on en.wikiquote, 'Albert Camus'; translator not named on the page consulted
suggested_refs: La Peste, Gallimard, 1947

stops.name: Beccar, the white house above the river
stops.date_confidence: attested at country level: es.wikipedia records the 1949 tour of Brazil, Argentina and Chile. The stay at Villa Ocampo is attested in victoria_ocampo.journey.json, whose pin is inherited unchanged; the date of the stay itself is not established in any source reached, and the month here orders the segment.
stops.campa: Already ill again, he crosses the Atlantic for a lecture tour of Brazil, Chile, and Argentina. North of Buenos Aires, on the bluff above the brown river at Beccar, he stays in Victoria Ocampo's house: the villa where Tagore convalesced and Stravinsky rehearsed, with its galleries and its planted gardens running down toward the water. The crossing and the schedule wreck him. He returns to France with the tuberculosis active and spends much of the next two years in bed. It is the only time he stands on Argentine ground.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, Elortondo 1811, Beccar, San Isidro
Camus's Journaux de voyage, covering the 1946 and 1949 crossings

stops.name: Paris, L'Homme révolté
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the publisher; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He publishes L'Homme révolté in 1951, an essay that follows the rebel from Sade through Saint-Just, Hegel, Bakunin and Nechayev to the camps, and argues that a revolution which accepts murder in the name of a justice still to come has already lost the thing it rebelled for. He writes it against Stalinism at a moment when much of the French intelligentsia will not hear a word said against the Soviet Union. The reviews are hostile from the first week and stay hostile.
stops.quote_source: L'Homme révolté (1951), as quoted on en.wikiquote, 'Albert Camus'; the page consulted renders it with a dash rather than a comma
suggested_refs: L'Homme révolté, Gallimard, 1951

stops.name: Paris, the quarrel with Sartre
stops.date_confidence: attested for the exchange and the year; the month orders the segment. The pin marks the Saint-Germain-des-Prés milieu the two men shared, not a single site, since no single site is recorded for the rupture.
stops.campa: Les Temps modernes lets the book sit, then hands it to Francis Jeanson, who dismisses it as bad philosophy by a man who has not read enough. Camus replies in a letter addressed to Monsieur le Directeur, declining to name Sartre at all. Sartre answers over his own signature, in print, and spares him nothing: the poverty he came from, the pride, the moralism, the aggrieved tone. The two men, friends since 1943, never speak again. Sartre goes on writing about him for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Francis Jeanson's review and the Camus-Sartre exchange in Les Temps modernes, 1952

stops.name: Paris, the letter to the Argentine ambassador
stops.date_confidence: attested in victoria_ocampo.journey.json, from which this pin and date are inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo is arrested in Buenos Aires and held in a cell in San Telmo. Word crosses the Atlantic within days. Camus, who has been her guest at the house in Beccar, drafts a letter of protest in his own hand and carries it himself to the Argentine embassy. Aldous Huxley and Waldo Frank raise a committee for the writers imprisoned in Argentina; Gabriela Mistral cables Perón directly; Nehru applies pressure through Delhi. He will lend his name this way again, for Spanish republicans, for Hungarians, for men under sentence of death. She is released.
suggested_refs: The 1953 international writers' committee for Victoria Ocampo's release

stops.name: Paris, the cost of the double life
stops.date_confidence: attested for the breakdown and the hospitalization in 1953, per Britannica, and for the attribution made within the family; the month orders the segment. Specifics that circulate about the treatment are not carried here, having no source in the verified pool.
stops.campa: Francine Camus breaks down in 1953 and is hospitalized for months. The cause named inside the family, and by Camus himself, is the affair with María Casarès, carried on publicly enough that literary Paris knows and privately enough that his wife is expected not to. He withdraws: almost no new work for three years, few appearances, a guilt he writes down only in notebooks. In 1954 he takes the apartment at 4 rue de Chanaleilles in the seventh arrondissement where he will live until he dies.
suggested_refs: 4 rue de Chanaleilles, Paris VII, Camus's home from 1954

stops.name: Algiers, the appeal for a civilian truce
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the exact day and the hall, which the sources reached do not name; the episode itself is widely reported and dated to January 1956.
stops.campa: With the war a year old and bombs going off in cafés, Camus returns to Algiers and stands up in a hall to ask both sides for one thing: that civilians be left out of it, that neither the French army nor the FLN kill people who are not fighting. Outside, a crowd of European Algerians chants for his death. Inside, the FLN men who helped arrange the meeting have their own use for it. He gets his truce from nobody, and the hall empties into a street where the killing has not paused.
suggested_refs: The Appel pour une trêve civile en Algérie, Algiers, January 1956, later printed in Chroniques algériennes

stops.name: Paris, the monologue in Amsterdam
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: La Chute is published in 1956: a monologue delivered in an Amsterdam bar by a former Paris lawyer who explains, over six evenings, how he came to see that his goodness was theatre, that he did not go in after the woman who fell from the bridge, and that the way to live with the knowledge is to confess first and accuse everybody afterwards. It is the funniest book he writes and the least merciful. Readers take it for a settling of accounts with Sartre. It looks more like one with himself.
stops.quote: Do not wait for the Last Judgment. It takes place every day.
stops.quote_source: La Chute (1956), as quoted on en.wikiquote, 'Albert Camus'
suggested_refs: La Chute, Gallimard, 1956

stops.name: Stockholm, the Nobel Prize
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the award. The citation is paraphrased rather than quoted: nobelprize.org returned 403 to every fetch attempt, so no exact citation text could be verified.
stops.campa: On the tenth of December the King of Sweden hands him the Nobel Prize in Literature, given for work that throws light on the problems of the human conscience in his time. He is forty-four, one of the youngest laureates the prize has had, born in a settler village in Africa to a mother who cannot read a line of what he has written. He tells the hall that art is not a solitary pleasure and that a writer cannot work apart from the people who make history and suffer it.
suggested_refs: The Nobel Prize in Literature 1957 and Camus's Stockholm banquet speech

stops.name: Stockholm, the Algerian student at the Maison des étudiants
stops.date_confidence: attested in the wording reported by Dominique Birman of Le Monde, who was in the room on 12 December 1957. The famous tramway version ('If that is justice, then I prefer my mother') is a later popular reconstruction, not the reported words, and is not quoted here.
stops.campa: Two days after the ceremony, at a meeting with students, an Algerian stands up and attacks him for what he has not said about the war. Camus answers him in front of the room: that he has always condemned terror, that he must also condemn a terrorism practised blindly in the streets of Algiers which could strike his mother or his family, and that he believes in justice but will defend his mother before justice. Le Monde's correspondent is present and writes the words down. They will travel in a shorter, harder form about a tramway.
stops.quote: J'ai toujours condamné la terreur... Je crois à la justice, mais je défendrai ma mère avant la justice.
stops.quote_source: Camus at the Maison des étudiants, Stockholm, 12 December 1957, as reported by Dominique Birman in Le Monde and cited on fr.wikipedia, 'Albert Camus'
suggested_refs: Dominique Birman's Le Monde report of the Stockholm student meeting, December 1957

stops.name: Uppsala, create dangerously
stops.date_confidence: attested; sv.wikipedia cites the Uppsala lecture of 14 December 1957. The images from the lecture are paraphrased rather than quoted, the text itself not having been opened in this pass.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth he lectures at the university under the title The Artist and His Time, printed afterwards as Create Dangerously. He tells the students that the writers of his century do not get the quiet of the tower. They are chained to a galley that stinks and carries too many overseers, and art on that deck is not an ornament. Every generation before his believed it was called to remake the world; his own knows it will not remake it, and may have the larger job of keeping the world from destroying itself. The lecture is given four days after the ceremony in Stockholm.
suggested_refs: 'L'artiste et son temps' / 'Create Dangerously', lecture at Uppsala University, 14 December 1957

stops.name: Lourmarin, the house bought with the prize
stops.date_confidence: attested for the purchase in 1958 with the prize money; the month orders the segment. That René Char recommended the village is standard in the literature and is not confirmed in the sources reached; a related claim, that Char shared his Paris building, was checked and dropped.
stops.campa: With the prize money he buys a house at Lourmarin, a village under the Luberon in the Vaucluse that he first saw before the war. It is the first property he has ever owned. The light is Mediterranean, the stone holds the heat, and the country is near enough to Algeria in feel that he can work there. He installs his family, walks, and writes most of Le Premier Homme in this house: a book about his father, his mother, and Belcourt. Friends say they have not seen him like this in ten years.
suggested_refs: Camus's house at Lourmarin, Vaucluse, bought 1958

stops.name: Paris, Dostoevsky at the Théâtre Antoine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the production in January 1959; the day orders the segment. Details of the staging and of a negotiation for a state theatre are standard in the literature and were not verified here.
stops.campa: In January his own adaptation of Dostoevsky's Demons opens at the Théâtre Antoine, directed by him, running most of an evening. He has carried the novel since he was twenty and calls it one of the four or five books he would keep. The production is a critical success, and he is in negotiation for a theatre of his own in Paris. He tells friends he is finished with the essay and nearly finished with the novel, and that he means to spend what working life remains to him on a stage.
suggested_refs: Les Possédés, Camus's stage adaptation of Dostoevsky, Théâtre Antoine, Paris, January 1959

stops.name: Villeblevin, the plane tree at Le Grand Fossard
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date, the place and the deaths. The road was the Route nationale 5, renumbered RN 6 later and D606 since 2006, which is the source of the 'Nationale 6' in the secondary literature. The car's model is contested, FV3B in fr.wikipedia and FV2 in en.wikipedia, so it is left unnamed. The unused train ticket is repeated everywhere and confirmed nowhere reachable.
stops.campa: He has a train ticket to Paris in his pocket. On the third of January his publisher and friend Michel Gallimard offers the car instead, and on the fourth, on the straight stretch of the Nationale 5 at the place called Le Grand Fossard outside Villeblevin, the Facel Vega leaves the road at speed and hits a plane tree. Camus is killed instantly. He is forty-six. Gallimard dies five days later in a Paris clinic; his wife and daughter, in the back, survive. In the mud beside the wreck lies a satchel holding a hundred and forty-four handwritten pages of an unfinished novel about a boy from Belcourt whose father died before he could remember him.
suggested_refs: The commemorative stele at Villeblevin, Yonne
Giovanni Catelli's contested claim, published 2013, that the KGB sabotaged the car, unsubstantiated and rejected by the standard accounts

stops.name: Lourmarin, the grave in the village cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial at Lourmarin. Sartre's eulogy is attested; the English sentence quoted is the standard rendering of it, not a verified transcription from the original France-Observateur text.
stops.campa: He is buried on the sixth of January in the small cemetery at Lourmarin, in a village he had owned a house in for two years, four thousand kilometers from the quarter he wrote about all his life and from the mother still living in it. The stone carries his name and two dates. Sartre, who has not spoken to him since 1952, writes the obituary and does not qualify a word of the praise. Francine, who survives him by many years, is laid beside him. The herbs of the Luberon come up over both stones within a season.
stops.quote: He represented in this century, and against History, the present heir of that long line of moralists whose works constitute perhaps what is most original in French letters.
stops.quote_source: Jean-Paul Sartre, obituary of Camus, January 1960, in the standard English rendering
suggested_refs: The cemetery of Lourmarin, Vaucluse
The 2009-2010 proposal to move Camus's remains to the Panthéon, opposed by his family and not carried out

stops.name: Paris, the first man in print
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1994 publication, edited by Catherine Camus; the month orders the stop.
stops.campa: Thirty-four years after the mud at Villeblevin, Gallimard publishes Le Premier Homme from the recovered manuscript, edited by his daughter Catherine, who was fourteen when he died. It is unlike anything else he finished: unguarded, unrevised, the notes to himself still standing in the margins. A poor boy in Belcourt, a deaf mother, a grandmother with a whip, a schoolmaster named Germain, and a father buried in Brittany whom the son goes at last to find, and discovers is younger than he is.
suggested_refs: Le Premier Homme, Gallimard, 1994, edited by Catherine Camus from the manuscript recovered at Villeblevin
